segments.text: I mean, what is it going to take?

segments.text: I mean, it's the biggest thing, the best historical parallel I can draw is Chernobyl.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: So after Chernobyl, the Soviet Union decided to convince everybody that there had been no medical fallout from all that radioactivity.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: And when people came forward with clear problems, doctors were told to tell them they have phobia, they have radiophobia.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: And they tried to make that last, and it lasted actually for two years.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: But then there was just so much blowback because so many injuries.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: And when you had kids being born, babies being born with fish tails, you had calves with their leg was next to their ear, you could only get away with that for so long.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: And even the Soviet Union and its totalitarian system arguably collapsed over the lies of Chernobyl.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: And I think the lies that have been spun out in defense of this mass medical experimentation of horrific failure, I think as the injuries accumulate and people start asking the right questions and people start making the right inquiries and enough conscientious doctors and nurses continue to come forward, it will at some point reach a critical mass that the system collapses.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: And I think the system will regret it because it will lead to people never trusting them for generations because of what they've done.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
